CausalChain: Fibrotic liver environment leads to increased matrix stiffness -> matrix stiffness activates integrin receptors and FAK signaling in TAMs -> FAK signaling raises HIF1α levels and alters metabolic pathways (e.g., enhanced glycolysis) -> metabolic reprogramming drives M2 polarization and secretion of immunosuppressive/angiogenic factors -> M2 TAMs promote tumor progression and therapy resistance; therefore, disrupting the integrin-FAK-HIF1α axis should reverse TAM polarization to an M1 phenotype.
Hypothesis: Targeting the integrin‐FAK‐HIF1α mechanotransduction axis in the liver tumor microenvironment will disrupt the stiff matrix‐induced metabolic reprogramming of TAMs, converting them from an M2 immunosuppressive phenotype to an M1 pro‐tumor immune state, thereby enhancing the efficacy of immunotherapeutic interventions in hepatocellular carcinoma.
Abstract: Tumor‐associated macrophages (TAMs) play a critical role in the progression of liver cancer, especially through their dynamic polarization states, metabolic reprogramming, and response to the physical properties of the tumor microenvironment. Notably, increased matrix stiffness—a hallmark of fibrotic or cirrhotic livers—has been implicated in driving TAMs toward a pro‐tumoral, immunosuppressive M2 phenotype. Concomitantly, mechanotransduction pathways stimulated by matrix stiffness, such as integrin‐mediated FAK activation, have been linked with upregulation of hypoxia‐inducible factor 1α (HIF1α) and subsequent metabolic shifts favoring glycolysis and fatty acid oxidation. We propose that disruption of this mechanotransduction/metabolic axis may reprogram TAMs to adopt a more pro‐tumoral M1 phenotype, thereby enhancing anti‐tumor immunity and improving responses to current immunotherapies targeting liver cancer.
